## Overview

The Souliotes were an Orthodox Christian Albanian tribal community in Souli, in Epirus, from the 16th century to the beginning of the 19th century. They originated from Albanian clans that settled in the highlands of Thesprotia and established an autonomous confederation over neighbouring villages in the mountainous areas of Epirus. At the height of its power, in the second half of the 18th century, the confederacy consisted of up to 4,500 inhabitants, although Souliot leaders estimated approximately 20,000 inhabitants in 1800. The Souliotes spoke the Souliotic dialect of Albanian and learnt Greek through interaction with Greek-speakers. Their historical importance lies in their resistance to Ottoman rule, their organization through patrilineal clans, and their participation in the Greek War of Independence, after which they settled in the newly established Greek state and assimilated into the Greek nation.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The Souliotes wore red skull caps, fleecy capotes over their shoulders, embroidered jackets, scarlet buskins, slippers with pointed toes and white kilts. The source does not distinguish everyday from ceremonial dress, nor does it describe women’s clothing, belts, jewelry, or separate forms of dress for particular occasions.

### Architecture

Souliote houses were essentially fortified towers placed in strategic positions so that they could be defended from attacks originating from other fortified towers. Churches also had embrasures. The sources identify the four principal settlements as Souli, Avariko, Kiafa and Samoniva, collectively called the *tetrachori*, and describe additional villages as an outer defensive ring.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do mention weapons, guns and ammunition in connection with warfare.

## Music & performance

The material does mention the Rhomaic (Greek)-Albanian dictionary composed in 1809 mainly by Markos Botsaris and his family members, and the diary of Fotos Tzavellas, composed during his captivity by Ali Pasha in 1792–1793. These are linguistic and historical documents rather than descriptions of musical performance. The sources also state that the decisions of the Souliot general assembly were not written down but agreed upon through the oral pledge of *besë*, which was central to agreements within Souliot society and with outsiders.

## Festivals & rituals

Religious affiliation is described as Orthodox Christianity: the Souliotes followed the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople and were members of the Rum millet.

The sources do describe political and military gatherings. Heads of clans met in the general assembly known in Greek as Πλεκεσία, a term linked to the Albanian *pleqësia*, or council of elders. The assembly was held in the open courtyard next to the church of St. George in Souli. It resolved disputes, formulated tribal laws, arbitrated between clans, and enforced the council’s decisions. The oral pledge of *besë* bound the heads of clans to the assembly’s agreements. Blood vengeance was another core social practice, connected with honour, dishonour, clan property, and customary justice.

## Foodways

They state that the Souliote economy was based on small-scale subsistence pastoralism, constrained by limited grazing grounds, and that pastoral communities engaged in raiding partly because of environmental conditions and lack of means of subsistence.

## Oral tradition & literature

The first historical accounts of Souliote rebellious activity date from 1685, while much information about earlier attacks and origins was preserved through oral stories. Perraivos based his account of the first attack against Souli on oral stories he collected and proposed that it occurred in 1721, although archival sources place the campaign more likely in 1731–33. Another attack, said in oral history to have occurred in 1754, is confirmed by archival sources and recorded in a text in the Church of St. Nicholas of Ioannina.

Oral agreement was central to Souliot political life. The decisions of the *pleqësia* were not written down but were accepted through *besë*. This concept formed the basis of agreements within Souliot society and agreements with outsiders, including hostile forces during wartime.

## Language & religion

The Souliotes spoke Albanian and used the Souliotic dialect, while also learning Greek through communication and exchanges with the mostly Greek-speaking population of surrounding areas. William Martin Leake recorded that Souliot men spoke Albanian at home and that all men could speak Greek, while many women could speak Greek as well. The closest existing variant of Souliotic Albanian is identified with the speech of Anthousa (Rapëza) and Kanallaki, although the dialect is spoken by only a few people in modern times.

The Rhomaic (Greek)-Albanian dictionary composed in 1809 contains Albanian vocabulary influenced by Greek, Turkish, Italian and other languages. Of 1494 Albanian words, 361 are identified as Greek loanwords, 187 as Turkish, 21 as Italian and two as loanwords from other languages. The Souliotes followed the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople and belonged to the Rum millet. They were Orthodox Christians. Their correspondence with Christian and Muslim leaders was written in Greek or translated from Greek.
